anquetil-zend-avesta-vol3:
Tome Three, from 1771, completes Anquetil-Duperron's Zend-Avesta in French. Later Pahlavi writings join the older Avestan texts in this close. His life of Zoroaster also finds its place in the volume.

Three tomes first opened the Persian sacred books to Western readers. Scholars argued over their worth, yet the door never closed again. The name of Zoroaster entered Europe's thought through this brave work. Its flaws are plain, but so is its vast, founding role. Oriental study in the West counts this set among its first great monuments. Later, better versions all build on the road Anquetil cut.
austin-lectures-jurisprudence-1863-vol3:
A third volume of Austin's Lectures appeared in 1863, after his death, drawn from his manuscripts. It holds notes and fragments that never became finished lectures. Sarah Austin, his widow, guarded his papers and saw them into print.

The fragments range over sovereignty, utility, and the science of legislation, in Austin's terse manner. Readers see the system still growing, with doubts and second thoughts left in. The volume serves as sequel to The Province of Jurisprudence Determined, his one finished book. For students of legal theory, these rough pages show a powerful mind at work without polish or pretense.
borlase-dolmens-ireland-1897-vol3:
Book three of The Dolmens of Ireland, from 1897, closes Borlase's survey of stone tombs. The first books listed the tombs county by county. This last part steps back and compares them. Borlase sets the Irish tombs beside like tombs in other lands.

He weighs who built them, when, and what rites they served. Myths and old tales tied to the stones get a close look too. A full list of sites ends the work for ease of use. The three books still form the base text for the study of Irish dolmens.
bracton-note-book-maitland-1887-vol3:
Volume Three of Bracton's Note Book completes Maitland's 1887 edition with the remaining plea-roll cases and the indexes. With this volume, the full casebook behind Bracton's treatise stands in print. Maitland closes the work he began as a young scholar.

The last cases run through land pleas, appeals of felony, and the work of the eyre courts. Indexes of names, places, and matters tie the three volumes together. Students can now trace a dispute or a judge across the whole set. The edition remains a bedrock source for thirteenth-century English law and for the craft of legal history itself.
campbell-popular-tales-west-highlands-18: J. F. Campbell's set of West Highland tales moves to its third part in this book, from the work of 1860. His team took the tales down in Gaelic, just as old folk told them by the fire. The set as a whole runs to four parts. The tales here keep the same wild, sea swept air as the first two parts. Seal folk, sea maids, and the heroes of old song share the Highland store. The part holds its place in the chain of the set.
coke-reports-1777-vol3:
The third volume of Wilson's 1777 Coke's Reports carries the case law further through the courts of Elizabeth and James the First. Coke's reports were already classics by the time Wilson re-edited them, their authority in court second only to statute. Each volume added another layer of precedent to the common law's growing structure.

Property, royal prerogative, and personal liberty all come before the courts in these pages. The great issues of the age are not debated in essays but decided in lawsuits, one dispute at a time. Coke records the arguments in detail, sometimes adding his own gloss on what the law should be. The volume shows the heroic age of the common law from inside the courtroom, in the words of the judge who more than any other defined it.
degroot-religious-system-china-vol3:
Volume Three of de Groot's system, from 1897, treats demon lore and sorcery. The dark side of Chinese religion fills this part of the work. Evil spirits haunt roads, homes, and bodies in the world he maps.

Exorcists fight back with charms, swords, noise, and fierce rites. De Groot records their wars with the same care he gives high faith. He draws on texts, priests, and tales heard in the streets. The shadow world behind the calm Confucian front stands revealed here. Few Western books match its depth on China's fear of spirits and demons. The cases he gathers range from grim to strangely comic by turns.
dutt-agni-purana-vol3:
Volume 3 of Dutt's Agni Puranam, from 1904, sets out law and statecraft. The fire god's scripture serves here as a manual for kings. Counselors, allies, foes, and war each get sharp, brief rules.

A king learns how to choose ministers and test their true loyalty. Treaties, spies, and the just conduct of war fill the chapters. Tax, forts, and the care of the treasury get the same care. The political sense of ancient India speaks in these crisp maxims. Dutt's clear English keeps the throne-room wisdom sharp and usable today. The maxims echo the famed tradition of Kautilya's statecraft in spirit.
dutt-garuda-purana-vol3:
Volume 3 of Dutt's Garuda Puranam, from 1908, completes his English version. A wide store of old lore fills this final part of the work. Medicine, omens, and gems stand beside rites and sacred tales.

The signs by which the wise read the world get patient treatment. Cures, charms, and rules for gifts and vows round out the survey. The purana closes like a handbook of old India's useful knowledge. Dutt keeps the tone plain and the matter well in order. Readers leave with a sense of how one book served many daily needs. The whole set shows the purana as both scripture and handbook.
frazer-totemism-and-exogamy-1910-vol3:
Frazer's third volume, published in 1910 with the rest of his treatise, turns from totemism itself to its partner, exogamy. The rule that people must marry outside their clan or group stood behind many marriage systems, and Frazer wanted its origin.

He examines totemic taboos, the bans on touch, food, and speech that guarded clan boundaries. Then he traces how such rules might have grown into the full clan system. The evidence is drawn from peoples on every continent, arranged for comparison. Read with the other volumes, this one shows the ambition of the project: one scheme to explain kinship worldwide.
freneau-poems-1907-vol3:
Pattee's third volume, printed at Princeton in 1907, completes the collected Poems of Philip Freneau. The title page repeats his standing title, Poet of the American Revolution. Later verse and the editor's notes fill this closing part of the set.

By his last years Freneau had become an elder figure in American letters. He kept writing on the sea, the land, and the republic he had helped imagine into being. Read as a whole, the three volumes lift from neglect the chief American poet of the 1700s. Scholars still rely on Pattee's work when they trace the start of a national poetry.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-1882-vol3: Jacob Grimm's study of German myth moves to its third part in Stallybrass's English text. The work as a whole is the base text of German myth, drawn from a life of work. Grimm set out to trace one world of belief through all its tribes. The third part holds the survey on its long course through gods, rites, and folk belief. Its notes pile quote on quote from sagas, laws, and charms in the old tongues.
holdsworth-history-english-law-1922-vol3:
Volume Three of Holdsworth's History, in the 1922 edition, treats the medieval common law itself. The courts and the profession take shape in these pages. Holdsworth follows them from the Angevin reforms to the close of the Middle Ages.

He describes the rise of the legal profession: serjeants, apprentices, and the Inns of Court. The forms of action, the jury, and the law of land and crime develop under his hand. Holdsworth's gift is order: a wilderness of records becomes a clear story. This volume completes the medieval part of the great history that lawyers still cite by his name alone.
kent-commentaries-american-law-1832-vol3:
Volume Three of Kent's Commentaries, in the second edition of 1832, turns to real property. Land law was the heart of private law in Kent's America. He lays out its feudal roots and its American changes with his usual order.

Feudal tenures, estates, titles, and conveyances in land fill the volume. Kent shows how English doctrines bent to fit a country of free farms and new states. His treatment of future interests and remainders guided courts for decades. Lawyers cited 'Kent' the way they cited scripture. The volume rewards anyone tracing how the law of land crossed the Atlantic and took root.
lamb-works-lucas-vol3:
Books for children fill the third volume of Lucas's 1903 Lamb edition. At its head stand the Tales from Shakespear, where Charles and Mary Lamb retold twenty plays in plain prose. The contents run from The Tempest and A Midsummer Night's Dream through Hamlet and Othello to Pericles.

Young readers met the Bard first through these clear retellings, and many still do today. The volume also holds The Adventures of Ulysses, Charles Lamb's version of Homer's wanderer for young readers. Grace and kindness mark the writing throughout, the same gifts that made the Lambs' essays so widely loved.
las-casas-historia-indias-vol3:
Hispaniola lies stripped bare in Volume 3 of Las Casas's great history. The 1875 printing carries the conquest onward from the islands. Spanish eyes now turn toward the mainland and its rich kingdoms.

Las Casas saw much of this himself as a young colonist. His later change of heart gives the telling a sharp, guilty edge. He piles up proof year by year, town by ruined town. Gold lust, slave raids, and mass death mark the advance he records. The case grows longer and darker with every chapter in this somber book. Las Casas spares neither king nor colonist in his charges.
marston-works-bullen-1887-vol3:
Bullen's 1887 Works of John Marston closes with this third volume, printed in London like the first two. Its contents open with Eastward Ho, then move to The Insatiate Countess, and end with poems and satires. The listed pieces include The Metamorphosis of Pygmalion's Image and The Scourge of Villainy.

These later works show Marston near the end of a short and stormy stage career. Soon after, he left writing behind and became a priest. Read as a set, the three volumes keep the full voice of a fierce writer. They give modern readers his mature plays and verse in one scholarly edition.
middleton-works-dyce-1840-vol3:
Dyce's third volume of Middleton's Works, from 1840, carries the collection through the middle of the canon. Middleton wrote alone and with partners, for the boys' companies and the great public stages alike. His range can look startling between two covers.

Tragedy and comedy stand side by side here, as they did in the repertory of his day. Middleton's great themes return: lust, money, disguise, and the thin skin between respectability and ruin. Dyce's notes trace sources and old stage history for each piece. The volume keeps the middle of the edition's promise, a complete Middleton for the price of patience.
neumann-reden-gotamo-buddhos-vol3:
With its third volume in 1921, Neumann's Die Reden Gotamo Buddhos completes the Mittlere Sammlung in German. The closing talks of the Majjhima Nikaya round out one of the great labors of early Western Buddhism. Neumann worked largely alone, and the finished set changed what German readers could know of the Buddha.

Late discourses in the canon often turn to the monks' training and the path's end. In Neumann's flowing German they reached scholars and seekers alike. The three volumes together remain the foundation of the Pali canon in German, a bridge built by one translator.
sahagun-historia-general-vol3:
Conquest, told by the conquered, fills Volume 3 of Sahagún's history. Bustamante printed the book in 1829 as part of the General History. Nahua survivors recount the fall of their world in their own words.

Omens come first, then the strangers land on the coast. Siege, plague, and hunger close around proud Tenochtitlan in the telling. The fall of the city lands with grief no victor's account can match. Sahagún lets the victims speak, and their voice haunts each page. Many call this the most moving book in the whole Florentine Codex line. Its grief has lost none of its force.
satow-tasj-vol3:
Volume Three of the Asiatic Society of Japan's Transactions covers 1874 to 1875. Ernest Satow and his circle of pioneers fill its yearly harvest. Their papers treat Japan's history, language, and customs with fresh zeal.

Satow's study of pure Shinto's revival stands out in this volume. Other papers map coasts, plants, words, and old tales as they go. The writers work in a Japan just opened to the wider world. Each paper feels like a dispatch from unknown country being charted. Western study of Japan is being built here, paper by paper, year by year. The volume's mix of zeal and fact charms as much as it teaches.
story-commentaries-constitution-1833-vol:
Volume Three completes Story's Commentaries of 1833 with the judiciary, the states, and amendments. Story was himself a sitting justice, which gives the volume special weight. The set closes with the forms of legal process under the Constitution.

He explains federal court power, the Bill of Rights, and the limits the Constitution sets on state laws. Story also reviews how amendments should be made and read. His closing pages urge citizens to guard the Union as their fathers' great work. The three volumes together formed the standard American constitutional treatise until modern casebooks took its place in the schools.
thorpe-northern-mythology-1851-vol3: Benjamin Thorpe closed his great set of north folk tales with this third part in 1851. The set as a whole bears the name Northern Mythology. Thorpe was the lead English scholar of the old north in his day, at home in its tongues. The third part rounds out his store of the tales and rites of the north folk. With the first two parts, it gives English readers the full sweep of his hoard. The set stays a base source for the folk lore of Scandinavia in English.
